An e-commerce browser direct object storage upload is easy to accept and surprisingly hard to own. The decision changes when customer files must expire, stay private, and remain deletable on your terms.

articles.author: Abanoub Kerols
articles.description:
npm install express
npm install
npm run dev
npm publish

But knowing these commands is very different from understanding what NPM is actually doing.
When you run:
npm install

NPM is not simply downloading some files.
It is solving a dependency graph, resolving versions, communicating with a registry, validating package metadata, building an installation tree, generating or updating a lockfile, running lifecycle scripts, and storing packages in a local cache.
And when you run:
npm publish

you are not simply uploading a folder.
You are creating a versioned package artifact that can become a dependency of thousands of other applications.
Understanding these internals changes how you think about:
package.json
package-lock.json
semantic versioning
dependency conflicts
node_modules
npm scripts…
articles.title: NPM Under the Hood: How Dependency Management, Lockfiles, Workspaces, Publishing & Security Really Work

articles.description:
Short answer: Send large generated report images from the browser straight to object storage with a short-lived presigned PUT, but issue that permission only after authenticating the customer and selecting the correct US or EU bucket. Treat CORS as a browser permission check, signing as an exact-request contract, and regional placement as a separate data-control decision. Mixing those three planes is what makes this incident drag on.
The operational rule is direct: reproduce the failing preflight first, then compare the eventual PUT byte for byte with what the signing service authorized. Don't widen CORS until the upload works. A broad policy can hide an origin or header mismatch while also expanding who can attempt writes.

articles.author: Mike Vu
articles.description:
A security monitor that can be switched off quietly is worse than none, because it still looks reassuring. This post covers how MacSentry, my open-source Mac monitor, tries to make silencing it noisy: telling a reboot apart from kill -9, two processes that watch each other, an append-only log, a dead man's switch, and a Telegram detail that lets malware delete your alerts if you are not careful.
The goal is not to be unstoppable. Someone with root can, given time, stop any local monitor. The goal is that the attempt itself gets reported, from outside the machine, before it succeeds.
Anything stored only on the Mac can be cleaned up by whoever gets in. So every finding is sent to Telegram the moment it happens, and the local log is a second copy, not the primary record.
Delivery has to surv…
articles.title: Making a Mac security monitor hard to silence

The site publishes a small queue file. Each morning, Make reads it, keeps only today's items, and sends them to Buffer. Buffer then posts them in the evening, Japan time, which is morning in the US.
Only published posts are in the queue. If a post is still a draft, its announcements stay out, so nothing points to a page that does not exist yet.
The stack is Make (free plan), Buffer (free plan, three channels) and Buffer's GraphQL API. The site is a static Astro site on Cloudflare.
